verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
verse.sanskrit: क्वासे क्व च गमिष्यामि कोऽन्वहं किमिहास्थितः / कस्मात्किमनुशोचेयमित्येवं स्थापयेन्मनः
verse.line: In grief, ask: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I? Let that steady you.
verse.translation: 'Where was I before? Where will I go? Who am I, really, and why am I here? Why should I grieve, and for what?' Ask these, and steady the mind.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
verse.misuse: These questions are for steadying grief, not for dismissing it; mourning is natural.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asked the sage Ashma how to bear the loss of his family and wealth. Ashma told him to ask where he came from, where he is going, and who he is. These questions steady the mind in grief. Days do not come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
verse.for_you: The house is quiet now. Let that silence hold the questions of where you came from and where you are going. Let them steady you before you reach for the Gita.

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.sanskrit: दिवसास्ते महान्तस्ते संपदस्ताः क्रियाश्च ताः । सर्वं स्मृतिपथं यातं यामो वयमपि क्षणात् ॥
verse.line: Those days, those people, that wealth, those deeds are memories now. We too will pass soon.
verse.translation: Those days, those great people, that wealth, those deeds: all have passed into memory. We too will go in a moment.
verse.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
verse.misuse: Not a call to despair; it wakes Rama up to what matters now.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

verse.meaning: Rama, the young prince, has just returned from years of exile to find his father dead. He is standing in the palace, surrounded by the trappings of power, and everything feels hollow. He tells the sages that those days, those great people, that wealth, and those deeds are memories now. We too will pass soon. It is a raw admission that the world he knew is gone and that his own life is slipping away. He does not yet know what to do with this emptiness, but he names it honestly. This is not despair.
verse.for_you: In this quiet house, you feel the weight of all that has passed into memory. You do not need another forwarded verse. You could sit with this honest naming of what feels empty, and let it wake you to what might matter now.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.sanskrit: देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा । तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
verse.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where grief has paralyzed him. He points out that just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The wise are not bewildered by this. What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. The body is a vessel that changes, but the self within is never born and never dies. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
verse.for_you: In the quiet house, you feel the weight of what has passed. This verse asks you to hold on to the part of you that does not change, even as the world around you does.

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

verse.meaning: The Chhandogya Upanishad speaks of a truth that lives in the heart. We visit this truth every night in deep sleep, yet we do not know it. The text compares our own self to buried gold. People might walk over a hidden treasure every day and never find it, carried away by what is not true. The verse asks us to stop walking past what is already here. It says the treasure is not lost. We simply do not know where to look. This is the ground you stand on now.
verse.for_you: The house is quiet, but you are not empty. You are walking over a treasure you do not yet know. Let the silence show you what is already here, beneath the noise of what has passed.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna opens the teaching on knowing him fully.
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचमय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः । असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु ॥
verse.line: Keep your mind attached to me, lean on me, keep practising. You will come to know me fully.
verse.translation: Hear, Partha, how with your mind attached to me, practising yoga and taking refuge in me, you will know me fully, without doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, opening the teaching on knowing him fully. He tells Arjuna to keep the mind attached to him, to lean on him, and to keep practising. This steady practice will lead to full knowing, without doubt. The verse does not ask for a single moment of perfect focus. It asks for a thread that stays held through the day. This is how you come to know what is already here.
verse.for_you: Take the Gita and read the first chapter as if you are hearing it for the first time. Let the silence between the lines teach you what the words do not say.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna begins his ladder of practices with the simplest instruction.
verse.sanskrit: मय्येव मन आधत्स्व मयि बुद्धिं निवेशय । निवसिष्यसि मय्येव अत ऊर्ध्वं न संशयः ॥
verse.line: Rest your mind in me, settle your thinking in me, and you will live in me.
verse.translation: Fix your mind on me alone, let your understanding settle in me; from then on you will dwell in me. Of this there is no doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Years after the war, Krishna turns to Arjuna and offers a single, quiet instruction. He does not ask for grand gestures or complex rituals. He asks Arjuna to rest his mind entirely on him, to let his understanding settle there, and then to dwell in him. This is not a ladder of many steps. It is one act of letting go, of fixing the attention on one thing until the rest of the world falls away. In the silence of your house, this is the practice he offers.
verse.for_you: The house is quiet now. Let that silence be the place where you rest your mind. You do not need to fill it with noise or forward shlokas. Just let your thinking settle in the quiet. That is your practice today.

story.title: Lakshmana's private question
story.story_hook: Years after the war, Lakshmana found his brother sitting alone and finally asked the question he had carried all along.
story.summary: After the war and his coronation, Rama is sitting alone when Lakshmana bows and asks how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama teaches him that knowledge, not ritual alone, frees a person, and that faith and a teacher make one steady as a mountain.
story.lesson: Even the closest companion needs to ask; with faith and guidance, you can become steady.

story.teaser: Years after the war, Lakshmana found Rama alone and asked his question
story.for_you: Lakshmana asked his brother for clarity when the war was over and the kingdom was won. You too have lived through the great events of your life, and now you have the space to ask what comes next. Find a teacher or a text that speaks to your own confusion, and let it steady you.

script: The house has grown very quiet since your wife passed. The children call on Sundays, and the rest of the day belongs to you. You are looking for something deeper than the shlokas you have been forwarded, and you want to read the Gita properly.

King Janaka asked the sage Ashma how to bear the loss of his family and wealth. Ashma told him to ask where he came from, where he is going, and who he is. These questions steady the mind in grief. Days do not come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you. And Ashma replied:
क्वासे क्व च गमिष्यामि कोऽन्वहं किमिहास्थितः / कस्मात्किमनुशोचेयमित्येवं स्थापयेन्मनः.
In plain words: In grief, ask: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I? Let that steady you.

This is the work of grief. It is not a problem to fix, but a place to stand. The sage does not ask you to ignore what is missing. He asks you to steady the mind by turning it toward what is true. Where did I come from? Where am I going? Who am I? These are not puzzles to solve. They are the ground that holds you when the ground has shifted.
Sit with the silence in the house. Let it ask the questions for you. Do not reach for the Gita to escape this quiet. Let it be the space where you meet what is true.

depth.life: The house is very quiet after your wife passed away. The children call on Sundays, but the rest of the time is a long stretch of silence. You have time now, and you want to read the Gita properly. This is the first real step into that search.
depth.points: Grief is the pain of what you did not want. The days that are gone will not return. You ask where you came from and where you are going because the loss has made the path unclear.
depth.practice: Sit in the quiet room where your wife was. Ask yourself, where was I before this? Let the silence answer that.
depth.question: What is the first thing that comes to mind when you ask where you were before this?
